title: Emotional responses to music: the need to consider underlying mechanisms
key_findings: Target article (BBS 31(5) 559-575): research had neglected the mechanisms by which music induces emotion; proposes six mechanisms beyond cognitive appraisal (brain stem reflex, evaluative conditioning, emotional contagion, visual imagery, episodic memory, musical expectancy).
practical_applications: A music brief must say WHICH mechanism we rely on (e.g. contagion via tempo/timbre, expectancy via a build), not just 'make it emotional'.
limitations: Theoretical; commentaries contest parts. Abstract-level access.

title: From everyday emotions to aesthetic emotions: towards a unified theory of musical emotions
key_findings: Revised framework with eight mechanisms: Brain stem reflex, Rhythmic entrainment, Evaluative conditioning, Contagion, Visual imagery, Episodic memory, Musical expectancy, Aesthetic judgement (BRECVEMA).
practical_applications: Checklist for music direction: which of the 8 does the cue use?
limitations: Physics of Life Reviews 10:235; snippet/abstract level.

title: A review of music and emotion studies: approaches, emotion models, and stimuli
key_findings: Review of 251 studies: self-report dominates; ~70% use discrete or dimensional emotion models; stimuli lean on a small set of familiar Western classical pieces.
practical_applications: Results generalise poorly to Thai pop, lo-fi or library music; test our own cues on our audience.
limitations: Music Perception 30(3) 307-340; abstract only.

title: Sweet Anticipation: Music and the Psychology of Expectation
key_findings: ITPRA theory: five expectation response systems - Imagination, Tension, Prediction, Reaction, Appraisal.
Devices such as syncopation, cadence, meter, tonality and climax exploit these responses; accounts for chills, laughter, awe.
Critics (e.g. Zilberg, Leonardo 2007) question universality claims from an ethnomusicology view.
practical_applications: Build tension (uncertainty) before a reveal, reward with a predictable resolution on the product shot; a 'wrong' surprise works for comedy.
limitations: Publisher page and reviews only; Western tonal bias.

title: Modeling tonal tension
key_findings: Tonal Pitch Space model predicts listeners' tension ratings from prolongational structure, pitch-space distance, surface dissonance and voice-leading attraction; extended to chromatic music.
practical_applications: Tension rises with distance from the home chord and dissonance; resolution = return home. Use at endings.
limitations: Music Perception 24(4) 329-366; summaries only; Western tonal music.
Check 2026-11-25: the Zenodo PDF previously linked is Wagner (2014) 'Cognitive Models of Tonal Tension', a University of Amsterdam student paper that reviews this model - not the original article.

title: Universal recognition of three basic emotions in music
key_findings: Mafa listeners (Cameroon) with no Western music exposure recognised happy, sad and scared/fearful Western piano excerpts above chance (about 2/3 happy, ~1/2 sad and fearful per press reports).
Authors warn against the 'universal language of emotion' idea.
practical_applications: Broad happy/sad/scary cues travel across cultures; finer moods (nostalgia, kreng-jai warmth) do not necessarily.
limitations: Current Biology 19(7) 573-576; 21 participants per coverage; summary-level access.

title: Mode and tempo relative contributions to 'happy-sad' judgements in equitone melodies
key_findings: Mode and tempo each affect happy-sad judgements; tempo was the more salient cue.
practical_applications: If we can't change the track's mode, tempo/energy is the stronger lever for 'happy vs sad'.
limitations: Cognition & Emotion 17:25-40; abstract-level summary.

title: Effects of musical tempo and mode on arousal, mood, and spatial abilities
authors: Husain, G.; Thompson, W. F.; Schellenberg, E. G.
key_findings: 36 undergraduates; Mozart K.448 as MIDI in 4 versions: 165 vs 60 bpm x major vs minor.
Tempo changed arousal but not mood; mode changed mood but not arousal; spatial-task scores followed arousal/mood (arousal-mood account of the 'Mozart effect').
practical_applications: Two independent knobs: tempo = energy/arousal, mode = valence/mood. Brief them separately.
limitations: Small sample; one piece; Western students.

title: Communication of emotions in vocal expression and music performance: different channels, same code?
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 104 vocal-expression and 41 music-performance studies; emotions are communicated with similar cue patterns (tempo/rate, loudness, pitch, timbre) in voice and music.
practical_applications: Match VO prosody and music cues (both fast/bright for joy, slow/soft/low for sadness) so they don't fight.
limitations: Psychological Bulletin 129:770-814; secondary summaries only for cue details.

title: The relationship between musical structure and perceived expression (Oxford Handbook of Music Psychology, 2nd ed.)
key_findings: Any structural factor (tempo, loudness, pitch, timbre, mode, rhythm, harmony...) can point to several emotions; effects are additive or interactive.
Clearest results for basic auditory/motion variables (loudness, timbre, pitch, tempo); typical musical variables less clear.
practical_applications: Write briefs in tempo/loudness/register/timbre first, harmony second.
limitations: Chapter abstract only.

title: The emotional connotations of major versus minor tonality: one or more origins?
key_findings: The major-positive / minor-negative valence association is psychologically robust in Western tonal music but has no single accepted explanation; Parncutt compares six partly related theories.

Theories: dissonance (minor passages rougher / less harmonic on average); alterity-markedness (major and positive emotion are the common norm, minor and negative the marked 'Other'); uncertainty (minor triad has a more ambiguous root; minor scale has three forms because degrees 6 and 7 vary); speech (minor scale degrees 3 and 6 are lower than expected, like sad speech); salience of flats; familiarity/cultural learning (differences emerged by accident in the 14th-16th centuries and were reinforced by composers).
Conclusion: there are arguments for and against each theory; the truth may be a mixture - not immediately clear which to privilege.
practical_applications: Minor = sad is a learned Western-tonal association, strong for our audience (Thai pop is largely Western-tonal) but not universal.
limitations: Theoretical review of Western tonal music; does not establish cross-cultural universality.

title: The impact of background music on adult listeners: a meta-analysis
authors: Kämpfe, J.; Sedlmeier, P.; Renkewitz, F.
key_findings: 97 studies analysed (from 189 articles); global effect is null because specific effects cancel out.
Background music vs none: disturbs reading (all 8 studies negative, mean r = -.11, n = 680), small negative effect on memory, positive on emotional reactions and sports.
Memory for advertisement content: negligible slight negative (r = -.05, 7 studies, n = 930).
Music tempo influences the tempo of activities done while listening.
practical_applications: Music under on-screen text or VO slightly hurts comprehension; music does help mood. Use it, but keep it simple and low under information.
limitations: Psychology of Music 39(4) 424-448; heterogeneous small studies; adults only.

title: The psychoacoustics of the irrelevant sound effect
key_findings: Irrelevant sound effect (ISE): memorising visually presented lists is reliably impaired by background sound that participants are told to ignore, at moderate levels; speech or speech analogues produce by far the largest effects (unfamiliar speech raised serial-recall errors by about 50% on average in the authors' data).
Noticeable spectral change over time is a necessary condition for an ISE; level change by itself is not.
FM-tone study (24 participants, FM rate 0-50 Hz): disruption is non-monotonic with a maximum near 4 Hz (where perceived fluctuation strength also peaks), but no FM tone disrupted as much as speech.

Table 1 re-tabulates earlier studies: music can produce almost equally large effects as speech (signals of sufficient spectro-temporal complexity); Salame & Baddeley (1989) vocal music produced larger effects than instrumental music.
No current model (cognitive or psychoacoustic - fluctuation strength, speech transmission index) captures all the data.
practical_applications: Sung lyrics and choppy, changing music under VO compete with the words more than a steady pad; prefer instrumental, smooth beds.
limitations: Invited review, Acoustical Science and Technology 35(1):10-16; lab serial-recall tasks, not video comprehension.

title: Effects of background music on phonological short-term memory
key_findings: As re-tabulated in Ellermeier & Zimmer 2014 (Table 1): vocal music disrupted serial recall more than instrumental music.
practical_applications: Historical anchor for 'vocal music disrupts verbal memory more than instrumental'.
limitations: Bibliographic only; findings not checked against the original.
Original not read; finding comes only from the Ellermeier & Zimmer 2014 review.

title: Impact of background music on reading comprehension: influence of lyrics language and study habits
authors: Sun, Y.; Sun, C.; Li, C.; Shao, X.; Liu, Q.; Liu, H.
key_findings: N=90 students of one sports university in Shandong (45 habitual music listeners, 45 not); Mandarin pop, English pop, no music: music with lyrics hurt reading comprehension.

90 college students in East China (50 female; 45 habitual music-listeners, 45 non-listeners; 30 per group: Mandarin pop, English pop, no music): music with lyrics reduced reading comprehension vs no music.
Comprehension dropped most when lyrics were in the same language as the text; accuracy was lowest with native-language (L1) lyrics for both listeners and non-listeners.
Non-listeners were hurt more; habitual listeners were much less distracted. Results support the duplex-mechanism account of auditory distraction.
Effect held even though the music was slow-tempo (contrast: Thompson et al. 2012 found fast, loud instrumental music disrupts reading more than slow).
practical_applications: For Thai text-heavy carousels/reels: no lyrics, especially not Thai lyrics, under reading or VO.
limitations: One sample of Chinese students, reading tasks (not video watching); a corrigendum has been published (not read).
Spot-check U3 2026-11-25 applied.

title: Sound advertising: a review of the experimental evidence on the effects of music in commercials on attention, memory, attitudes, and purchase intention
key_findings: Review (Journal of Media Psychology) of experiments on music in commercials and attention, memory, attitude and purchase intention; findings on recall are mixed.
practical_applications: Music in ads is not automatically positive; fit and attention matter.
limitations: Seen only as a search snippet; title partly from snippet.

title: An ad's musical congruity with the brand fires purchase intent (WARC)
key_findings: Summarises effects of 10 types of music-brand congruity on purchase intent, brand attitude, recall and affect.
practical_applications: Musical fit (genre, tempo, mood matching brand and picture) is the main variable to brief.
limitations: Paywalled trade article; snippet only. Some studies find incongruent music raises attention and recall.

title: Congruence-Association Model and experiments in film music: toward interdisciplinary collaboration
key_findings: CAM: viewers build a coherent narrative from audio and visual channels; structural congruence (shared accents/timing) steers visual attention, association supplies meaning.
practical_applications: Accents in music that coincide with visual accents direct the eye; the music's mood colours how the scene is interpreted.
limitations: Music and the Moving Image 8(2) 5-24; summaries only.

title: Use music and sound effects from the Audio Library (YouTube Help)
key_findings: Creative Commons tracks require crediting the artist in the video description (copy text provided); standard-licence tracks need no attribution.
Audio Library content is copyright-safe on YouTube and won't get Content ID claims; monetisable in YPP.
The page does not state rules for use outside YouTube.
practical_applications: OK for YouTube uploads; for FB/IG/TikTok use only CC BY tracks with credit, or platform libraries.
limitations: Terms change; check per track licence.

title: About CC Licenses
key_findings: Six licences: BY, BY-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC, BY-NC-SA, BY-NC-ND; all require attribution; NC forbids commercial use; ND forbids sharing adaptations; CC0 waives rights (public domain dedication).
practical_applications: Shop content is commercial: avoid NC tracks. Cutting a track to picture may count as an adaptation, so avoid ND tracks for music we edit.
limitations: Not legal advice; whether a sync edit is an 'adaptation' should be checked in the licence legal code.

title: About the Commercial Music Library (TikTok Ads help)
key_findings: Page last updated July 2025: the Commercial Music Library is a pre-cleared global library of 1 million songs, free for businesses to use in content on TikTok.

Businesses cannot use the general music library commercially; the CML is to be used for all commercial TikTok activity - organic content (including duet, react, stitch), video ads and branded content.
Using other users' original sounds or other licensed sounds in business content requires your own licence check.
practical_applications: Business accounts posting promos on TikTok should pick from the CML in-app.
limitations: Help page; detailed CML terms (separate page) not read; use outside TikTok is not granted by this page.

title: Meta Sound Collection terms (as summarised by secondary sources and Instagram help)
key_findings: Secondary summaries: licence covers commercial or non-commercial use but only inside content on Meta products; one Instagram help page says library music is for personal, non-commercial use - conflicting.
practical_applications: Use Sound Collection only for FB/IG content; never export it to TikTok/YouTube; check terms before paid ads.
limitations: Conflicting statements; primary terms not read.

title: Copyright Act B.E. 2537 (1994), English translation
key_findings: s.19: copyright lasts for the author's life plus 50 years; ss.20-22 give other terms (e.g. sound recordings, audiovisual works).
s.4: 'sound recording' excludes a film soundtrack; 'audiovisual work' includes its soundtrack.

s.32 para 1: use is not infringement if it does not conflict with normal exploitation and does not unreasonably prejudice the owner; para 2 lists purposes (research/study non-profit, personal use, criticism with acknowledgement, news, teaching...).
Performers' rights (s.44) last 50 years from the performance/recording (s.49); s.45 remuneration for commercial use of recorded performances.
practical_applications: A shop promo is commercial use: none of the s.32 purposes cover using a popular Thai song in an ad. License it or use cleared libraries.
limitations: Unofficial translation; amendments up to Copyright Act (No. 5) B.E. 2565 (2022) exist (IP Thailand) and were not checked. Not legal advice.

title: Edit to the beat in Final Cut Pro for Mac
key_findings: Final Cut Pro Beat Detection analyses a music clip and shows a beat grid of song parts (big structural transitions), bars and beats; edit points snap to the grid when snapping is on.
It can trim a music clip to the length of a video edit without perceptible breaks; Apple advises a 4/4 clip for the most accurate grid.
Toggle with Clip > Enable Beat Detection (Option-B).
practical_applications: Confirms the craft practice of editing on beat/bar grids; our beat-clip pipeline uses librosa for the same.
limitations: Vendor documentation (Final Cut Pro for Mac); accuracy not independently tested.
